period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story: Meena and Her Paper Boats

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the scene by asking children if they have ever floated something in water and what happened. This brief warm-up draws on children's own play experiences and orients them to the story's setting.

The teacher reads the story aloud from the textbook (pp. 56–58), pausing at key moments — Meena's anger, the boy's admission, and the shared boat-floating — to model expressive reading. Children follow along in their books.

The class does a shared reading of the same pages, with the teacher and children reading alternate paragraphs aloud together. The teacher encourages clear pronunciation and attention to punctuation cues like exclamation marks.

The teacher leads a brief whole-class discussion: 'What surprised you most in this story?' Children respond orally in one or two sentences. The teacher accepts and affirms varied responses without correcting for content.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the class's first encounter with the full story text, so an unhurried read-aloud that models intonation — especially for Meena's angry dialogue — helps children distinguish emotional registers in narrative. Watch for children who conflate Meena's anger with unkindness; the story's resolution shows her choosing generosity despite the anger.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think (pp. 58–59): answer three short questions about Meena's play, anger, and help.
Let us think (p. 59): judge four True/False statements about Meena and the boy.

time_bands.activity: Having read the story of Meena and the paper boats together, the teacher re-reads pp. 57–58 aloud at a measured pace while children listen with books open. This re-encounter prepares children to answer factual questions with confidence.

Let us think — A. ("three short-answer questions about Meena's play, anger, and her help to the boy"): the teacher poses each question orally, children discuss in pairs for a moment, then volunteers share answers aloud. The teacher scribes accurate answers on the board for children to copy into their books.

Let us think — C. ("True or False statements about the boy's motive, Meena's reaction, the boy's skill, and the paper colours"): children work individually, writing T or F beside each statement. The teacher then reveals answers one by one, asking children to point to the sentence in the story that supports each verdict.
The teacher invites children to share which statement surprised them most and why. This brief reflection consolidates story comprehension before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often mark the statement 'Meena had only white paper' as True without checking the story — the prose specifically mentions coloured paper in different sizes, so nudging children to point to the evidence in the text is particularly valuable here. Encourage children to speak their reasoning aloud rather than simply calling out T or F.

periods.activity_title: Speaking: Paper Things, Games, and Picture Stories

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think + Let us speak (p. 59): guided small-group talk about paper creations and favourite games.
Let us speak (p. 60): picture-series retelling of the 'Manish saves the ant' story to the class.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recalls the moment in the Meena story where she takes out coloured paper of different sizes to show the boy how to fold boats. The teacher asks children to think silently: 'What other things can you make with paper?'

Let us think — B. ("guided small-group discussion on paper creations and favourite games"): children talk in groups of three or four. After group discussion, one spokesperson per group shares two or three ideas with the class. The teacher lists paper creations on the board.

Let us speak ("picture-series retelling — Manish saves the ant"): the teacher walks children through the six pictures on p. 60, eliciting one-sentence observations picture by picture. Children then take turns retelling the whole picture story to a partner before two or three volunteers retell it to the class.

The teacher invites children to compare the two stories — how did both Meena and Manish show kindness? Children respond with one sentence each. The teacher affirms responses and closes the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may stay literal in the picture retelling, simply naming objects. Prompt them gently with 'And then what did Manish feel?' or 'Why do you think the ant needed help?' to nudge narrative sequencing toward cause and consequence. The comparison between Meena's and Manish's kindness is an oral bridge to the story's theme, not an assessed task.

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Pronouns He and She

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p. 61): fill in blanks with 'he' or 'she' for four sentence pairs.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes two sentence pairs from the story on the board — one using 'Meena' then 'she', and one using 'the boy' then 'he' — and asks children what they notice about the second sentences. This draws the pronoun concept directly from the story they know.

The teacher models two more examples with the class, choosing different names from the class itself (e.g. 'Priya has a pencil. _____ writes neatly.'). Children call out the correct pronoun and the teacher scribes it, narrating the reasoning aloud each time.

Let us learn — A. ("fill-in-the-blank sentences with 'he' or 'she' for Rani, Sahil, Durga, and Ranjit"): children complete the four items individually in their books. The teacher circulates, checking and prompting children who hesitate by asking 'Is this a girl's name or a boy's name?'

The teacher reads each sentence pair aloud and invites a child to say the correct pronoun before writing it on the board. Children check and correct their own work. The teacher briefly names the concept — 'we use she for a girl, he for a boy' — in plain language.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes write 'she' for names that are unfamiliar to them and default to guessing — guiding them to think about whether the name belongs to a girl or a boy in the sentence context, rather than memorising the name, builds transferable reasoning. Names like Durga may puzzle some children; accept a brief clarification without over-explaining.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p. 62): fill in blanks choosing on, under, or in for five picture-based sentences.

time_bands.activity: The teacher places or mimes placing a book on a desk, under a chair, and in a bag, saying each preposition clearly as the action happens. Children repeat the word after each demonstration. This physical warm-up anchors the three prepositions in body-memory before the textbook task.

The teacher asks children to open their books to p. 62 and look at the bedroom picture together. Walking through it class-by-class, the teacher points to each object and asks 'Where is the bat? Where is the bag?' Children call out what they see, using on, under, or in in a phrase.

Let us learn — B. ("fill-in-the-blank sentences choosing on, under, or in for the bat, bag, ball, car, and books in the bedroom picture"): children complete all five items individually. The teacher circulates and, for children who hesitate, points to the corresponding object in the picture rather than supplying the word.
The teacher reads each sentence aloud and asks the child who answered correctly to explain their choice in one sentence. Answers are confirmed on the board. Children check and correct their own work.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes confuse 'in' and 'on' when the picture shows an object resting inside an open container — for the ball in the box, encourage children to mime placing a ball inside a box to feel the distinction. The physical demonstration from the opening carries into this correction naturally.
materials: A book, a bag, and a chair (for the opening demonstration)

periods.activity_title: Writing: A Park Scene in a Few Lines

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p. 64): write a few lines about a park picture using eight given clue words.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws children's attention to the park picture on p. 64 and asks them to name what they can see. As children call out objects and activities, the teacher writes the eight clue words — park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, happy — on the board. This shared observation fills the vocabulary register children will draw on.

The teacher thinks aloud and writes one model sentence on the board using two of the clue words (e.g. 'Children are playing on the swings.'). The teacher then asks children to suggest a second sentence together, scribing it with the class's input. This modelled-writing demonstration shows children the sentence-level expectation.

Let us write — A. ("picture-prompted writing using the eight clue words to describe the park scene"): children write their own three or four sentences independently in their books. The teacher circulates, encouraging children who are stuck to point at one thing in the picture and say it aloud before writing it. Peer sharing of a sentence with a neighbour is invited midway if helpful.

Three or four volunteers read their sentences aloud. The teacher responds to each with one specific positive observation (e.g. 'You used the word enjoying very well.'). Children make any corrections they notice after hearing classmates.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often list items ('There is a slide. There is a see-saw.') rather than composing connected sentences — praising any attempt that uses a clue word in a full sentence, however simple, encourages the habit of complete expression. The goal is a few meaningful, connected lines, not a polished paragraph.

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Rangoli Art and Toys Crossword

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p. 63): follow six steps to draw a rangoli pattern on the dot grid.
Let us explore (p. 65): solve the toys-and-games crossword puzzle.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p. 66): talk to an elder at home and find out one game they played as a child; be ready to share the game with a friend.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly connects the session to the story's theme of games and making things with your hands — just as Meena demonstrated paper-folding, today children will make a rangoli and think about games. The teacher shows p. 63 and the six-step diagram.

Let us do — A. ("six-step rangoli on the dot grid"): the teacher walks through each of the six steps on p. 63 with the class, drawing on the board at the same pace. Children follow step by step in their books, using pencil. The teacher checks progress at steps 3 and 5 before children add colour if they choose.

Let us explore — B. ("toys-and-games crossword puzzle on p. 65"): children read each clue aloud with the teacher before attempting the answer. They work individually to fill the crossword grid. The teacher circulates and for children who are stuck, re-reads the clue slowly and mimes the object where possible.

The teacher reveals crossword answers by asking volunteers to call out each word. Children check their grids. The teacher briefly notes the homework invitation on p. 66 — to ask an elder at home about games — and explains children may share what they learn with a friend.

periods.teacher_notes: The rangoli step-by-step is a fine-motor and sequencing activity — children who struggle to copy the dot-grid pattern benefit from the teacher modelling on the board at a larger scale. For the crossword, 'marble' (Across 4) and 'ball' (Down 3 / Across — both share the same letter grid square) tend to confuse children; read those clues carefully together before children attempt them.

items.source_context: Meena's paper-boat play, her anger at the boy, his admission, and her generous teaching.
items.item_stem: Why did the boy keep overturning Meena's paper boats in the stream?

options.label: A
options.text: He did not like the colour of the paper.

options.label: C
options.text: He wanted to show Meena a better way to float boats.

options.label: D
options.text: He wanted to stop Meena from playing near the bridge.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student focused on Meena's location rather than the boy's stated motive.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student may have confused the boy's initial behaviour with Meena's helpful action later.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows the student may be inventing a detail not present in the story.

items.source_context: Meena's paper-boat play, her anger at the boy, his admission, and her generous teaching.
items.item_stem: After the boy admitted he did not know how to make paper boats, what did Meena do? Write two sentences in your own words.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Meena stopped being angry and decided to help the boy. She took out coloured paper in different sizes and showed him how to fold it step by step to make a boat.

items.source_context: Paper creations, favourite games, and the Manish-saves-the-ant picture story sequence.
items.item_stem: Look at the pictures on Textbook page 60. Which picture shows Manish helping the ant get to safety? Choose the correct description.

options.label: A
options.text: Manish picks up the ant with his hand and carries it home.

options.label: B
options.text: Manish places a paper boat in the stream so the ant can ride it to safety.

options.label: C
options.text: Manish throws a stone into the stream to scare the ant away.

options.label: D
options.text: Manish walks past the stream without noticing anything.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student did not observe the key action in the picture sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows the student may have recalled a different rescue scenario not shown in the pictures.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student invented an action not present in any picture.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture of the park on Textbook page 64. Choose any three of the words below and write one sentence for each word. Words: park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, happy.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any three grammatically complete sentences that use one clue word each and match what is visible in the park picture, for example: The children are playing in the park. They enjoy the swings and the slide. Everyone looks happy.

expected_elements: Names the setting (park) in at least one sentence.
Describes at least two activities shown in the picture.
Includes a feeling word such as happy or enjoying.

items.item_stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word from the brackets.
1. Kavya has a red umbrella. ________ carries it to school. (he / she)
2. The cat is ________ the table. (on / under)
3. Arjun loves football. ________ plays it every evening. (he / she)
4. The pencil is ________ the box. (in / on)
